a: the second vision
p: The Parables are a separate book, added after the Book of the Watchers (chapters 1–36).
b: Chapters 37–71 call themselves Enoch's "second vision." The first is the Book of the Watchers (chapters 1–36). Scholars call 37–71 the Book of Parables or the Similitudes. It is the only one of the five books inside 1 Enoch that has not turned up among the Aramaic fragments at Qumran, and no Greek of it survives. Everything we know of it comes from Ethiopic manuscripts, the oldest from the 1400s.

a: son of Jared, son of Mahalalel, son of Kenan, son of Enosh, son of Seth, son of Adam
p: The line runs backward from Genesis 5, so the reader knows which Enoch is speaking.
b: The list follows Genesis 5:3–18 in reverse. Ge'ez spells Kenan as Qaynan, like the Greek Kainan (Luke 3:37). Jude 14 makes the same point more briefly: "Enoch, the seventh from Adam." Naming the line ties these visions to the man who "walked with God" (Genesis 5:24), and it makes the claim of the book plain: this wisdom is older than the Flood.

a: the Lord of Spirits
p: The Parables' own name for God, used over 100 times, and almost nowhere else.
b: ʾƎgziʾa Mänafəst, "Lord of the spirits," is the favorite name for God in chapters 37–71 and is found almost nowhere else in 1 Enoch. Most scholars think it reworks "the LORD of Armies" (YHWH tseva'ot), the God who rules the hosts of heaven. 39:12 shows the link: the angels sing Isaiah 6:3, but "the LORD of Armies" has become "the Lord of Spirits," and "the whole earth is full of his glory" has become "he fills the earth with spirits." Compare "God of the spirits of all flesh" (Numbers 16:22).

a: the Holy One
p: Here a title of God, as in Isaiah's "the Holy One of Israel."
b: Ge'ez qədus, "holy one," could also mean an angel, since the angels are "holy ones" all through 1 Enoch. Here it is God, whose words Enoch passes on. The fuller title "the Holy Great One" belongs to the Book of the Watchers (see 1:3).

a: He has given me a share in eternal life
p: Enoch says he already has his share in eternal life. The Hebrew Bible says only that God took him.
b: Genesis says only, "Enoch walked with God. Then he was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). The Parables fill the gap: Enoch already holds his "share" (Ge'ez kəfl, a lot or portion) of eternal life, and in chapters 70–71 he is taken to heaven to receive it. Hebrews 11:5 agrees that Enoch was taken so that he would not see death. The idea of "eternal life" (Daniel 12:2) goes beyond anything Genesis says, but agrees with later Scripture.

a: Three parables
p: Not a story like Jesus's parables, but a lofty revealed speech, like Balaam's oracles.
b: Ge'ez məsale translates Hebrew mashal, a word that covers proverbs, riddles, taunt songs and prophetic oracles. Balaam "took up his mashal" (Numbers 23:7). The three "parables" here (chapters 38–44, 45–57, 58–69) are long visions about judgment, not short stories. The word may also hint that each vision compares heaven with earth. Older English books call them "Similitudes."

a: When the community of the righteous appears
p: The writers saw themselves as a small, hidden group of the righteous, waiting to be shown in the open.
b: The Parables speak for a group that calls itself "the righteous," "the holy" and "the chosen." Now they are hidden and oppressed. At the judgment they will "appear," and their oppressors will be driven off the land. The group is not named. Most scholars place it in Judea or Galilee around the time of Herod the Great or soon after, a people who felt crushed by rich landowners and their rulers.

a: It would have been better for them never to have been born
p: Jesus says the same of his betrayer (Matthew 26:24).
b: The saying is a Jewish way of describing a doom worse than death. Jesus uses it of Judas (Matthew 26:24; Mark 14:21). The Parables use it of "those who denied the Lord of Spirits," a phrase that keeps coming back (41:2; 45:2; 46:7; 48:10). Here "deny" probably means refusing to honor God by how one lives, not only by words.

a: hang on the Lord of Spirits
p: Their deeds depend on God, or, as some read it, are weighed by him.
b: The Ge'ez says the deeds of the chosen are "hung on" (səqul) the Lord of Spirits. The phrase comes back in 40:5 and 46:8. Most take it to mean "depend on, rest on." Some think the picture is a pair of scales, and translate "weighed by." The Plain keeps the picture.

a: those who hold the land
p: The villains of the Parables are the people who own the land.
b: "Those who hold the land" (or "the earth"; Ge'ez yäbs means dry land) is one of the Parables' names for the enemy, beside "the kings and the powerful." It may point to great estate owners in Herodian Judea, and to the kings who protected them. The promise is that the land will change hands: the "holy, righteous and chosen" will hold it (compare Psalm 37:11; Matthew 5:5).

a: the kings and the powerful
t: Who are "the kings and the powerful"?
p: Rome? Herod's family? Gentile kings in general? The text never names them.
b: The phrase runs through all three parables (46:4; 53:5; 54:2; 62:1–12; 63:1–12). Readers have suggested: (1) the Hasmonean kings, Jewish rulers of the first century BC; (2) Herod the Great and his sons, with the Roman officials behind them (the view of many today, partly because of 67:8–13); (3) Gentile kings in general; or (4) any tyrants in any age. Readers who take the book as prophecy, as the Ethiopian church does, can apply it to the unjust rulers of every age who will face Christ's judgment.

a: chosen and holy children will come down from the high heavens
p: Probably the Watchers of Genesis 6, described as they were before they fell.
b: Most scholars read this as the descent of the Watchers, the angels who married women (Genesis 6:1–4; see 1 Enoch 6:1–8). Enoch speaks before the Flood, so the event is still future for him, and the angels are called "chosen and holy" because they were holy before they sinned. A few read it differently: the souls of the righteous coming to join humanity, or a hope for angels living among people. The Ethiopic is not clear, and Charles thought the verse had been moved here from a Noah book.

a: Enoch received books of jealous anger and fury
p: The narrator suddenly speaks of Enoch in the third person.
b: The verse switches from "I" to "Enoch," one sign that 37–71 was put together from more than one source. The "books" are probably writings of judgment, the same kind of rebuke Enoch carries to the Watchers in 13:4–10 and 14:1–7. "Jealous anger" renders qənʿat, the zeal of a God who will not share his people (Exodus 20:5).

a: a cloud and a whirlwind snatched me up
p: Enoch's journey recalls Elijah's whirlwind and Enoch's own earlier ascent.
b: Ge'ez dämäna is "cloud" and näfas is "wind." Elijah went up "in a whirlwind" (2 Kings 2:11). In 14:8 clouds and winds lift Enoch to God's house. The New Testament uses the same picture: Jesus is taken up in a cloud (Acts 1:9), and believers will be "snatched up... in clouds" (1 Thessalonians 4:17).

a: They were asking, pleading and praying for the children of humans
t: The righteous dead pray for the living
p: The holy ones in heaven pray for people on earth. Churches differ on what this means.
b: In this vision the righteous who have died live with the angels and pray for those still on earth. Revelation shows the prayers of God's people rising before the throne (Revelation 5:8; 8:3–4) and the martyrs crying out (Revelation 6:10). Catholic and Orthodox Christians, including the Ethiopian church, ask the saints to pray for them, and read passages like this as support. Most Protestants hold that Scripture does not teach that the dead pray for the living, or that we should ask them to.

a: under the wings of the Lord of Spirits
p: A psalm picture of shelter, here a home in heaven.
b: "Hide me in the shade of your wings" (Psalm 17:8) and "beneath his wings you can take shelter" (Psalm 91:4) speak of God's protection. Ruth came "under the wings" of the God of Israel (Ruth 2:12). The Parables turn the picture into a place: the homes of the righteous lie under God's wings, near his throne.

a: My share has been there all along
p: Enoch's place was "settled" in advance before the Lord of Spirits.
b: Enoch says his portion in heaven was fixed ahead of time. The Parables speak this way often: the Son of Man is chosen and hidden before creation (48:3, 6), and the righteous are "chosen." Readers who stress God's choosing find support here; others note that the same book calls people to repent (50:2–3) and judges them by their deeds (41:1).

a: Those who never sleep
p: Angels who are always awake: the meaning of the Aramaic word for "Watchers."
b: Ge'ez ʾəlla ʾiyənawwəmu means "those who do not sleep." It describes the highest angels. The Aramaic name for the angels in 1 Enoch, 'irin (Daniel 4:13, 17), means "wakeful ones," which is why they are called "the Watchers" (see 1:5). In the Parables the phrase is used only of the good angels around the throne (39:13; 61:12; 71:7).

a: Holy, holy, holy is the Lord of Spirits. He fills the earth with spirits.
p: The seraphim's song from Isaiah 6:3, with "spirits" in place of "glory."
b: Isaiah heard the seraphim cry, "Holy, holy, holy is the LORD of Armies. Everything that fills the earth is his glory" (Isaiah 6:3). Here the song is reshaped to fit the Parables' name for God. Revelation 4:8 changes it too: "Holy, holy, holy is the Lord God, the Almighty." The song, called the Sanctus (Latin for "holy") or the Kedushah in Jewish worship, is still sung in synagogues and churches.

a: My face was changed
p: Seeing God's glory changes the seer's face, as with Moses.
b: Moses' face shone after he spoke with God (Exodus 34:29–35). Enoch's face is "changed" until he cannot keep looking. 71:11 goes further: there his spirit is changed. The Gospels use a related word for Jesus on the mountain, whose face "was changed" (Luke 9:29).

a: thousands of thousands and ten thousand times ten thousand
p: The same count of angels as Daniel 7:10 and Revelation 5:11.
b: Daniel saw "a thousand thousands" serving God and "ten thousand times ten thousand" standing before him (Daniel 7:10). Revelation 5:11 has "ten thousand times ten thousand, and thousands times thousands." The Parables lean on Daniel 7 more than any other passage. Here it is the count; in chapter 46 it will be the Ancient of Days and the one like a son of man.

a: four faces
p: Four angels of the presence, who stand nearest to God.
b: Ge'ez gäṣ means "face." Here it means an angel who stands in God's presence, before his face. Jewish writings speak of "angels of the presence" (Isaiah 63:9; Jubilees 1:27). Gabriel calls himself "the one who stands before God" (Luke 1:19). The number four may come from the four living creatures around the throne in Ezekiel 1, each with four faces.

a: the satans
p: Accusers, not yet the single Devil of later writings.
b: The Ge'ez plural säyṭanat shows how the Hebrew word satan, "accuser, adversary," could still be a job rather than a name. In Job 1–2 and Zechariah 3:1 "the satan" accuses people in God's court. Here a whole class of accusers tries to come before God, and an angel drives them back. Revelation 12:10 celebrates the day "the accuser of our brothers and sisters" is thrown down. In 53:3 and 54:6 one "Satan" leads them.

a: Phanuel
p: The fourth archangel. In chapters 9 and 20 the fourth is Uriel instead.
b: Fanuʾel is Hebrew Penuel, "face of God," the name Jacob gave the place where he saw God face to face (Genesis 32:30). It suits an angel of the presence. In 9:1 the four are Michael, Uriel, Raphael and Gabriel; the Parables put Phanuel in Uriel's place. In the Bible only Michael and Gabriel are named. Raphael is named in Tobit 12:15, a book Catholics and Orthodox read as Scripture.

a: holy Michael, who is merciful and slow to anger
p: The Bible names two angels. Enoch names four and gives each a job.
b: The 66 books name only Michael (Daniel 10:13; 12:1; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7) and Gabriel (Daniel 8:16; Luke 1:19, 26). Enoch adds Raphael, who heals (his name means "God heals"), and Phanuel, who leads people to repent. It also gives Michael God's own traits, "compassionate and gracious, slow to anger" (Exodus 34:6). Catholic and Orthodox churches honor Michael, Gabriel and Raphael as archangels; the Ethiopian church also honors Phanuel among its archangels. Most Protestants say no more about angels than Scripture names.
r: Daniel 10:13; Daniel 12:1; Jude 9; Revelation 12:7; Luke 1:19; Tobit 12:15; Exodus 34:6

a: how people's deeds are weighed on the scales
p: Judgment pictured as weighing, as in Daniel 5 and Egyptian art.
b: "you were put on a scale and found lacking" (Daniel 5:27); Job asks to be "weighed on honest scales" (Job 31:6). Egyptian tomb paintings show the heart of the dead weighed against a feather. The Parables use the picture again for the angels (61:8) and the stars (43:2). The point is that judgment is exact and fair.

a: locked storehouses
p: A Bible picture: God keeps the snow, hail and wind in storerooms.
b: "Have you entered the storehouses of the snow, or seen the storehouses of the hail?" God asks Job (Job 38:22). God "brings the wind out of his storehouses" (Psalm 135:7; Jeremiah 10:13). Enoch is shown what Job was told he could not see. The Parables return to this in 60:11–22 and 69:23.

a: by the oath that binds them
p: The sky keeps its order because God bound it with an oath.
b: The sun and moon "keep faith with each other" and never add to or subtract from their path. The Parables picture the order of the world as obedience to a sworn command, the hidden oath of 69:13–25. Jeremiah uses the fixed order of sun and moon as a pledge that God's covenant with Israel will last (Jeremiah 31:35–36; 33:20–21). The Astronomical Book (chapters 72–82) works out the paths in detail.

a: for blessing and for curse
t: Light for some, darkness for others
p: The same sky blesses the righteous and curses sinners.
b: The verse says the sun and moon serve both blessing and curse, light to the righteous and darkness to sinners. Some read it morally: those who keep God's calendar walk in light, while those who follow a wrong calendar sin without knowing it (compare 80:2–8). Others read it as a picture of judgment, like the plague of darkness that touched Egypt but not Goshen (Exodus 10:23).

a: he appoints a judge over them all
p: God appoints one judge for all, probably the Chosen One of the next chapters.
b: The Ge'ez says God "sees" (appoints) a judge. Charles thought the verse belonged after 41:2 or 42:3. Many readers think the judge is the Chosen One, who sits on the throne of glory and judges in 45:3 and 61:8. Others take "he judges them all" as God judging in person. The New Testament says God "has set a day when he will judge the world in the right way, through a man he has marked out for this" (Acts 17:31).

a: Wisdom found no place to live
p: A dark turn on the Bible's poems about Lady Wisdom.
b: In Proverbs 8 and Sirach 24 Wisdom is a woman who comes to live among people. Sirach says God told her to "pitch your tent in Jacob" (Sirach 24:8). This short poem says the opposite: Wisdom found no home on earth and went back to heaven, and Wrongdoing moved in. John's Gospel uses the same pattern for the Word: "He came to what was his own, and his own people did not welcome him" (John 1:11). The Parables promise that Wisdom will be poured out again through the Chosen One (49:1–3).
r: Proverbs 1:20–33; Proverbs 8:1–36; Sirach 24:8–12; Baruch 3:37; John 1:11; John 1:14; 49:1–3

a: like rain in the desert
p: Wrongdoing is welcomed the way rain is welcomed in a dry land.
b: The image is shocking on purpose. Rain and dew are blessings in the Bible (Deuteronomy 32:2; Hosea 14:5). Here people soak up wrongdoing as eagerly as thirsty ground soaks up rain. Wisdom looked for a home and found none; Wrongdoing found people it was not even looking for.

a: he calls each one of them by its name
p: Isaiah's picture of God the Creator calling the stars.
b: "The one who marches their army out by count and calls each one by name" (Isaiah 40:26); "He counts how many stars there are; he calls each of them by a name" (Psalm 147:4). Baruch 3:34–35 has the stars answer, "Here we are!" The Parables add a twist in 43:4: the stars stand for the names of the righteous.

a: These are the names of the righteous
p: The stars picture the faithful on earth, whom God knows by name.
b: The angel explains the vision as a "parable": the stars that obey their names are the righteous who believe. Daniel promises that those with insight "will gleam like the gleam of the dome of the sky... will blaze like the stars, for ever and ever" (Daniel 12:3). God promised Abraham children like the stars (Genesis 15:5). In 104:2 the righteous will "shine like the lights of heaven."

a: some of the stars rise and become lightning
p: An ancient attempt to explain lightning as fallen stars.
b: Ancient people did not know what lightning was. Some Greek thinkers thought it was fire squeezed out of clouds; some Near Eastern texts tied it to the stars. The Parables say some stars become lightning and stay that way. The verse may also carry a warning, since in the Book of the Watchers and the Dream Visions stars that leave their place stand for fallen angels (18:14–16; 86:1–3).

a: those who deny the name of the home of the holy ones
p: An odd phrase. It may mean denying the heavenly world where the holy ones live.
b: The Ge'ez reads "the name of the dwelling of the holy ones and of the Lord of Spirits." Some scholars think a word dropped out and read "the name of the Lord of Spirits and of the dwelling." Others take it as it stands: the sinners deny that there is a heaven, a home of the holy ones, at all, and so they deny any judgment to come. 45:2 fits that: they will go neither up to heaven nor down to earth.
orig: ይክሕዱ ፡ ስሞ ፡ ለማኅደረ ፡ ቅዱሳን (yəkḥədu səmo lämaḫdärä qədusan)

a: This is the second parable
p: Dillmann writes wäzkalʾ as one word; the EOTC Bible spaces it out.
b: Dillmann's text has wäzkalʾ məsale, with "and this" and "second" run together as one word. The EOTC Bible prints the same words with a word divider, wäz kalʾ məsale. Both say "this is the second parable," matching the count of three parables in 37:5, the end of the second at 57:3 and the start of the third at 58:1.

a: my Chosen One will sit on the throne of glory
t: The Chosen One on the throne
p: A judge on "the throne of glory": the phrase Jesus uses in Matthew.
b: Ge'ez ḫəruy, "Chosen One," echoes God's servant in Isaiah: "my chosen one; my soul is pleased with him" (Isaiah 42:1). Other texts enthrone humans (Ezekiel the Tragedian puts Moses on God's throne; the Testament of Abraham seats Abel as judge), and 1 Samuel 2:8 and Sirach 47:11 give a throne of glory to people God raises up. But a heavenly judge on "the throne of his glory" is shared mainly by the Parables (45:3; 55:4; 61:8; 62:5; 69:27) and Matthew, where the Son of Man takes "his seat on the throne of his glory" (Matthew 19:28; 25:31). Whether Matthew knew the Parables, or both drew on shared Jewish language, is much debated (see 62:5).

a: I will change heaven
p: Isaiah's "new heavens and a new earth."
b: God promises to change heaven and earth and make them a blessing. Isaiah 65:17 and 66:22 speak of "new heavens and a new earth," and Revelation 21:1 sees them. 2 Peter 3:13 waits for "new heavens and a new earth, where righteousness lives." In 45:5 the chosen will live on the changed earth, not only in heaven, as in Matthew 5:5.

a: one who had a head of days
p: Daniel's "Ancient of Days" in Ethiopic dress.
b: Ge'ez rəʾsä mäwaʿəl, literally "head of days," means one whose days are many, a very old one. It renders the "Ancient of Days" of Daniel 7:9 (Aramaic 'attiq yomin). From here on the Plain uses "the Head of Days" as a title. His head "white like wool" also comes from Daniel 7:9, and Revelation 1:14 gives the same white hair to the risen Jesus.

a: whose face looked like a human face
p: This is Daniel 7:13's "one like a son of man," now beside God.
b: In Daniel's vision "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom (Daniel 7:13–14). Daniel 7 itself explains the figure as "the holy ones of the Most High" (Daniel 7:18, 27). The Parables read him as one person, a heavenly figure who looks human yet is "like one of the holy angels." If the Parables are pre-Christian, as most scholars think, this is the earliest Jewish text we know to treat Daniel's figure as an individual judge.

a: that Son of Man
p: The first of three Ge'ez phrases for "son of man." All are "the Son of Man" in the Plain.
b: Here the Ge'ez is wäldä säbʾ, "son of people" (46:2–4; 48:2). Later the book also uses wäldä ʾəgʷalä ʾəmmäḥəyaw, "son of the offspring of the mother of the living" (from 62:7), and wäldä bəʾəsi, "son of a man" (69:29; 71:14). All three render Daniel's Aramaic bar 'enash, "a human being." The Ethiopic almost always says "that Son of Man," pointing back to the one first seen in 46:1. Whether this is already a title is debated: the Plain capitalizes it because the book treats it as naming one figure.

a: He will uncover all the storehouses of what is hidden
p: The Son of Man reveals hidden things, as God does in Daniel.
b: In Daniel, God "uncovers deep things and hidden things" (Daniel 2:22). Here the Son of Man does it. Colossians 2:3 says that in Christ "all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge lie hidden." The Son of Man is also "chosen" by God, joining two titles that the Parables use for one figure: the Son of Man, the Chosen One, the Righteous One and the Anointed One.

a: will rouse the kings and the powerful from their couches
p: Mary's song uses the same reversal: rulers off their thrones.
b: "He has pulled rulers down from thrones / and raised the lowly high" (Luke 1:52). The Parables turn the reversal into a court scene: the Son of Man drags kings off their couches and thrones. "Loosen the reins" pictures kings like horses whose bridles are cut. "Crush the teeth" comes from the Psalms (Psalm 3:7; Psalm 58:6).

a: where their kingdom came from
p: Rulers must admit that their power comes from God, as Daniel 4 and Romans 13 teach.
b: The kings fall because they will not humbly admit who gave them their kingdom. Daniel 4 makes the same point with Nebuchadnezzar, humbled until he knew "that the Most High is ruler over the kingdom of humankind" (Daniel 4:32). Paul says "There is no authority that does not come from God" (Romans 13:1), and Jesus tells Pilate the same (John 19:11). Here Enoch agrees closely with the 66 books.

a: worms will be their bed
p: The taunt against the king of Babylon in Isaiah 14.
b: "Under you, maggots make your mattress; worms are your bedcovers" (Isaiah 14:11), said of the proud king of Babylon brought down to Sheol. Isaiah 66:24 speaks of the worm that does not die, a verse Jesus quotes (Mark 9:48). "No hope of rising from their beds" may mean no resurrection to life for the wicked, as in 51:1–2 only the righteous are chosen.

a: the ones who judge the stars of heaven
p: An odd phrase. The stars may be the righteous, as in 43:4.
b: The Ge'ez says the kings "judge" (yəkʷennu) the stars of heaven. Charles and others thought the text was damaged. A better reading may be that "the stars" are God's holy people, as in 43:4 and Daniel 8:10, where a king "threw some of the stars to the ground and trampled them." Then the kings put the righteous on trial and raise their hands against God himself.

a: the houses of his congregation
p: Meeting places of the faithful: synagogues, or the writers' own groups.
b: Ge'ez məstəgubuʾ means "gathering, congregation." The Ge'ez is singular, "his congregation" (Charles made it plural). The houses may be synagogues, which were spreading through Judea and Galilee in the first century BC and AD, or the houses where the writers' own group met. 53:6 promises that the Righteous One will make "the house of his congregation" appear. Christian readers have often applied it to the church.

a: the blood of the righteous rose from the earth
p: From Abel's blood to the souls under the altar.
b: "Your brother's blood has a voice, and it is crying to me from the ground" (Genesis 4:10). In 9:1–10 the angels report the cries of murdered people. Here the blood of the righteous martyrs rises to God, and the angels join the prayer. Revelation 6:9–11 is very close: the souls under the altar cry, "how long until you judge the people who live on the earth and pay them back for our blood?" and are told to wait until their number is complete.

a: The books of the living were opened
p: Daniel's court scene; Revelation's book of life.
b: "The court sat, and books were opened" (Daniel 7:10). The Parables call them "the books of the living," close to the "book of life" of Psalm 69:28, Philippians 4:3 and Revelation 20:12. Revelation describes it this way: "books were opened. Another book was also opened: the book of life" (Revelation 20:12). In Enoch the books also record the deeds of sinners (81:1–4; 98:7–8).

a: the number of the righteous had been reached
p: A set number of the righteous must be reached before the end comes.
b: The Ge'ez reads "the number of righteousness had come." Most translators take it as "the number of the righteous," the full count of those who must suffer before judgment. Revelation 6:11 tells the martyrs to wait "until their fellow slaves and their brothers and sisters ... were complete in number too." 4 Ezra 4:35–37 has the souls of the righteous ask, "How long?" and hear that the end will come when the number is full.

a: the blood of the righteous had been avenged
t: The blood of the righteous, or of the Righteous One?
p: The Ge'ez is singular; the Plain reads it as a group.
b: In 47:1 and here the Ge'ez has the singular ṣadq: wädämä ṣadq, wädämu läṣadq, literally "the blood of the righteous one." Ge'ez often uses the singular for a whole class, and the same verses speak of "the prayer of the righteous" in the plural, so the Plain takes it as the righteous as a group. Some readers, Christian and scholarly, have taken it as the blood of the Righteous One, the title in 38:2 and 53:6.

a: a spring of righteousness that never runs dry
t: The spring that never runs dry
p: Water of life for the thirsty, as in Isaiah and John.
b: "All you who are thirsty, come to the water" (Isaiah 55:1). Jeremiah calls God "the spring of living water" (Jeremiah 2:13). Jesus says the water he gives "will become a spring inside him, of water leaping up into eternal life" (John 4:14), and Revelation promises "the spring of the water of life" without cost (Revelation 21:6). In 49:1 the same wisdom is "poured out like water."

a: Before the sun and the signs were created
t: Did the Son of Man exist before creation?
p: Was he there before the world, or only his name, in God's plan?
b: The verse says his name was named before the sun was made, and 48:6 says he was "chosen and hidden" before the world. Many scholars read this as real pre-existence: a heavenly being who existed before creation, as Wisdom does in Proverbs 8:22–31. Others read it as "ideal" pre-existence: God chose him and his name in his plan, as the rabbis said the name of the Messiah was among seven things made before the world (Talmud, Pesachim 54a). Christians compare John 1:1–3 and John 17:5.

a: the signs
p: Probably the signs of the zodiac, or the sun and moon as signs for seasons.
b: Ge'ez täʾämər means "sign, wonder." Genesis 1:14 says the lights in the sky "will be signs, and will mark the appointed times." Many take "the signs" here to be the constellations of the zodiac. The point is that the Son of Man's name came before anything in the sky.

a: He will be the light of the nations
p: The Son of Man takes on the work of Isaiah's Servant.
b: God says of his servant, "I make you a covenant of the people and a light to the nations" (Isaiah 42:6; 49:6). Simeon says the same of the baby Jesus (Luke 2:32), and Paul applies it to his mission (Acts 13:47). "A staff for the righteous" may echo Psalm 23:4. The Parables give the Son of Man several titles from Isaiah's Servant songs: chosen (Isaiah 42:1), righteous (Isaiah 53:11), hidden (Isaiah 49:2), and the light of the nations.
r: Isaiah 42:6; Isaiah 49:6; Luke 2:32; Acts 13:47; Isaiah 49:2; Isaiah 53:11

a: fall down and worship before him
t: Worship before the Son of Man
p: Does all the earth worship him, or God in front of him?
b: Ge'ez sägädä means to bow down, either in honor or in worship. The verse could mean that all people bow before the Son of Man, then praise the Lord of Spirits. 62:9 is clearer: the kings "worship" the Son of Man and "put their hope" in him. Philippians 2:10 says every knee will bow at the name of Jesus. Some scholars see here a Jewish precedent for Christian worship of Jesus (Boyarin); others think the bowing is royal homage and the worship goes to God alone (Hurtado). Christians who read Enoch, including the Ethiopian church, see Christ worshiped as God.

a: chosen and hidden in his presence
p: Like the arrow kept in the quiver in Isaiah 49:2.
b: "He made my mouth a sharp sword and hid me in the shade of his hand. He made me a sharpened arrow and tucked me away in his quiver" (Isaiah 49:2). The Son of Man is hidden until God reveals him to the chosen (48:7; 62:7). Paul speaks of "the mystery that was kept hidden for ages" and now revealed (Colossians 1:26), and 1 Peter 1:20 says Christ was "known in advance, before the world was founded," and "brought into the open in the last of the times."

a: it is his will that they live
p: A disputed last line: God's will for their life, or the one who avenges their lives?
b: The Ge'ez is wäfäqade konä läḥəywätomu. The Plain takes fäqade as "will, wish": it is God's will that they live, close to Charles's "according to his good pleasure." Several modern versions take the word as a noun for a person, "he is the one who seeks (or avenges) their lives," making the Son of Man the protector of the righteous. Both fit the context of 48:4–7.

a: his Anointed One
p: One of only two places where the Parables use the word "messiah."
b: Ge'ez mäsiḥ is the same word as Hebrew mashiach, "anointed," which gives English "Messiah" and, through Greek, "Christ." It appears only here and in 52:4. "The Lord of Spirits and his Anointed One" repeats Psalm 2:2, where the kings of the earth plot "against the LORD and against his anointed." The Parables apply the royal title to the same figure as the Son of Man and the Chosen One, showing that one Jewish group already combined these hopes.

a: In him lives the spirit of wisdom
t: The spirit on the branch of Jesse
p: Isaiah 11:2, the spirit that rests on the coming king, now on the Chosen One.
b: "The LORD's Spirit will come to rest on him, a spirit of wisdom and understanding, a spirit of counsel and strength, a spirit to know and to fear the LORD" (Isaiah 11:2). The Parables give that spirit to the Chosen One, and 62:2, if it speaks of the Chosen One (see the note there), adds Isaiah 11:4: the word of his mouth kills the wicked. So the Chosen One is also the king from David's line. The last phrase, "the spirit of those who have fallen asleep in righteousness," means he carries the hope of the righteous dead.

a: No one will be able to speak an empty word in his presence
p: Before this judge, lies and excuses are useless.
b: Jesus warns that people will give an account on judgment day "for every careless word" (Matthew 12:36). The Parables repeat the line (62:3; 67:9). The judge sees what is hidden, so no one can talk their way out. The same idea closes the kings' hopes in chapter 63, where their words of praise come too late.

a: He will let the others see it
p: A third group, neither righteous nor sinners, who can still repent.
b: Between the righteous and the sinners stand "the others." They see the righteous win, repent and give up "the works of their hands" (idols, or simply their deeds). They are saved "through his name," though in Dillmann's text without the "honor" of the righteous (50:3; the EOTC text gives them honor). Many think they are Gentiles who turn to God at the end, as in Isaiah 2:2–4 and 90:30. Others think they are Jews who had compromised. The chapter is unusual in apocalyptic writing for leaving a door open.

a: The Lord of Spirits will have mercy on them
p: Saved at the end by repentance alone: a hope the 66 books share, with limits.
b: In Dillmann's text the others have no merit ("no honor") but are saved by God's name and great mercy; the EOTC Bible says they will have honor (see the variant). Christians have compared the workers hired at the eleventh hour (Matthew 20:1–16) and the thief on the cross (Luke 23:42–43). But 50:4–5 sets a limit: after the judgment there is no more mercy for those who do not repent. Hebrews 9:27 likewise speaks of judgment after death, not a second chance. Readers differ on how wide the door is.

a: the earth will give back what was entrusted to it
t: The earth gives back its dead
p: One of the clearest Jewish resurrection passages, probably older than the New Testament.
b: The dead are like a deposit (Ge'ez maḫḍänt) left with the earth and Sheol, and they must be returned. Isaiah 26:19 says the earth will give birth to the dead, and Daniel 12:2 that many who sleep in the dust will wake. Revelation 20:13 has "the sea gave up the dead who were in it, and Death and Hades gave up the dead who were in them." 4 Ezra 7:32 uses almost the same words as Enoch. Here the passage agrees with the 66 books, and, if most scholars date it rightly, is earlier than most of the New Testament.

a: the place of destruction
p: Ge'ez ḫagʷl, "destruction," here a place of the dead like Abaddon.
b: Beside Sheol stands ḫagʷl, "destruction, ruin." It probably stands for Hebrew Abaddon, "Destruction," which the Bible pairs with Sheol (Job 26:6; Proverbs 15:11) and Revelation makes the name of the angel of the abyss (Revelation 9:11). Charles rendered it "hell."

a: the counsel of his mouth
p: Wise judgments from the Chosen One's own lips.
b: Ge'ez ḥəlina ʾafuhu is "the thought, counsel of his mouth." It may echo Isaiah 11:2 ("the spirit of counsel") and Isaiah 9:6 ("Wonderful Counselor"). The Chosen One both judges and teaches: his words reveal secrets of wisdom that God has given him.

a: the mountains will leap like rams
p: A line from the Passover psalm, Psalm 114.
b: "The mountains leapt like rams, the hills like young sheep" (Psalm 114:4). In the psalm creation jumps at the Exodus; here it jumps for joy at the resurrection. Isaiah 55:12 has the mountains break into song. The point is that the whole of creation shares in the joy when the dead are raised.

a: a mountain of iron, a mountain of copper, a mountain of silver, a mountain of gold
p: Like the metal statue of Daniel 2, these stand for the world's power.
b: Nebuchadnezzar dreamed of a statue of gold, silver, bronze and iron, crushed by a stone that became a great mountain (Daniel 2:31–45). The six mountains here are metals of wealth and of war. The angel says they will melt before the Chosen One (52:6) and be useless (52:7–9). The metals also recall the teaching of Azazel, who showed people how to work metal (8:1). Wealth and weapons are exactly what the kings of the Parables trust in.

a: soft metal
p: The Ge'ez word means "dripping" metal, perhaps tin or antimony.
b: Ge'ez näṭäbṭab comes from a verb meaning "to drip." It names some soft or easily melted metal, perhaps tin, antimony or an alloy. The same list of metals returns in 52:6, 65:7 and 67:4. Translators differ because the exact metal cannot be fixed from the word alone.

a: the authority of his Anointed One
p: A Messiah who rules on earth, as the Psalms and Prophets promise.
b: The second and last use of "his Anointed One" (see 48:10). His rule is "on the earth," not only in heaven, as in Psalm 2:8 and Daniel 7:14. Christians see this fulfilled in Christ, to whom "all authority in heaven and on earth" is given (Matthew 28:18). Jewish readers who take Enoch as a witness to Second Temple hope see here an expectation of a Messiah still to come.

a: like wax before the fire
p: The prophets' picture of God's coming.
b: "Like wax, the mountains melt away in the LORD's presence" (Psalm 97:5); "Under him the mountains melt... like wax near a fire" (Micah 1:4). 1:6 uses the same picture for God's coming at the start of 1 Enoch. Here the mountains melt before the Chosen One, and God's own coming is pictured as his.

a: not by gold and not by silver
p: Zephaniah's warning about the day of the LORD.
b: "Neither their silver nor their gold will be able to save them on the day of the LORD's wrath" (Zephaniah 1:18; compare Ezekiel 7:19). The Parables are a book for the poor and the oppressed: the rich trusted in wealth (46:7), and it will fail them. 1 Peter 1:18 says believers were ransomed "not with things that perish, silver or gold."

a: a deep valley with its mouth wide open
p: Probably the Hinnom Valley by Jerusalem, the root of the word "Gehenna."
b: Deep valleys of punishment appear in 26:4 and 27:1–3, where Enoch sees a cursed valley by Jerusalem. Joel 3:2, 12 speaks of the Valley of Jehoshaphat, where God judges the nations. The Valley of Hinnom, Hebrew Ge Hinnom, was cursed for child sacrifice (Jeremiah 7:31–32) and gave its name to Gehenna, the Gospels' word for hell (Mark 9:43). Here the nations' tribute pours into it, and it is never full.

a: will bring him gifts, presents and tribute
p: The nations bring gifts, as in the royal psalm.
b: "May the kings of Tarshish and the islands pay tribute. May the kings of Sheba and of Seba offer gifts" (Psalm 72:10). Isaiah 60:5–11 has the wealth of the nations flow into Jerusalem. "Him" is probably the Chosen One. Christians have long compared the gifts of the wise men (Matthew 2:11).

a: the angels of punishment
p: Angels who carry out God's sentences.
b: Ge'ez mälaʾəktä mäqśäft, "angels of punishment," appear again and again in the Parables (56:1; 62:11; 63:1; 66:1). The Bible has a destroying angel (Exodus 12:23; 2 Samuel 24:16) and angels who pour out the bowls of wrath (Revelation 16:1). Here they work for God, yet use "the tools of Satan," so Satan's work ends up serving God's justice.

a: the Righteous and Chosen One
p: Another title for the same figure, as in Acts.
b: Ge'ez ṣadq wäḫəruy joins two titles. "The Righteous One" (38:2) may come from Isaiah 53:11, "my righteous servant." In Acts the apostles call Jesus "the Righteous One" (Acts 3:14; 7:52; 22:14), and 1 John 2:1 does the same. "The house of his congregation" may be the gathered people of God, or a renewed temple.

a: the armies of Azazel
p: The leader of the fallen angels, met first in the Book of the Watchers.
b: Ge'ez ʾAzazʾel. In the Book of the Watchers he teaches people to make weapons and jewelry (8:1) and is bound in the desert until judgment day (10:4–6). The name is close to the "Azazel" of the Day of Atonement, to whom the scapegoat is sent (Leviticus 16:8, 10). In the Parables his "armies" are the fallen angels, and they are judged by the Chosen One (55:4).

a: They will cover their jaws with rough stones
p: The same punishment as Azazel's in 10:5.
b: In 10:5 Raphael is told to throw Azazel into a pit in the desert and cover him with "rough and jagged stones." Jude 6 and 2 Peter 2:4 speak of angels kept in chains in darkness for judgment, the same picture.

a: they became servants of Satan
p: Here the Watchers serve Satan. In the Book of the Watchers they fall on their own.
b: In chapters 6–16 the Watchers sin by their own choice, led by Shemihazah and Azazel, and Satan is not mentioned. The Parables link the two stories: the Watchers "became servants of Satan," the chief accuser (40:7; 53:3). The New Testament speaks of "the devil and his angels" (Matthew 25:41; Revelation 12:9), closer to the Parables. Genesis 6 says nothing about Satan at all.

a: In those days punishment will go out from the Lord of Spirits
t: A piece of a Noah book
p: From here to 55:2 the subject suddenly becomes the Flood.
b: Scholars have long noticed that 54:7–55:2, 60, and 65–69:25 tell of Noah and the Flood and break the flow of the Parables. 60:8 and 65:2 are spoken by Noah. A "Book of Noah" is named in Jubilees 10:13 and 21:10, and many think the editor of 1 Enoch drew on such a book. The Flood may be placed here as a pattern for the final judgment, as in Matthew 24:37–39.

a: The water above the heavens is male, and the water below the earth is female
p: An old Near Eastern picture of the waters mating, put to new use.
b: Genesis 1:6–7 separates the waters above the sky from the waters below, and at the Flood both burst open (Genesis 7:11). Here the two waters are pictured as male and female, joining again. Babylon's creation story, the Enuma Elish, begins with Apsu (fresh water, male) and Tiamat (salt sea, female) mingling. The Enochic writer uses the picture without any goddess: the waters obey God.

a: the Head of Days changed his mind
p: Enoch has God regret the Flood. Genesis has him regret making humankind.
b: Genesis says, "The LORD was sorry that he had made humankind on the earth" (Genesis 6:6), and after the Flood promises never again to strike every living thing (Genesis 8:21). Enoch goes a step further: God says the destruction was "for nothing" (Ge'ez bäkä, "in vain"), perhaps because sin came back after the Flood. Jewish and Christian teachers explain such language as God speaking in human terms (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Readers should note that the Ge'ez says more than Genesis does.

a: I will put a sign in the heavens
p: The rainbow of Genesis 9.
b: "My bow I have put in the clouds, and it will be the sign of a covenant between me and the earth" (Genesis 9:13). Enoch does not name the bow, but "a sign in the heavens" and "a pledge of faith... as long as heaven is above the earth" point to it. Compare the promise "as long as the earth lasts" (Genesis 8:22).

a: He will judge Azazel and all his company
p: The Chosen One judges the fallen angels. Paul says believers will judge angels.
b: In the Book of the Watchers God himself judges the Watchers (10:11–15; 16:1–3). Here the Chosen One does it, on God's own "throne of glory." Paul writes, "Do you not know that we will judge angels?" (1 Corinthians 6:3), and Jesus says the Father has given all judgment to the Son (John 5:22). Christians who read the Parables see Christ as this judge.

a: They held nets
p: The Ge'ez word usually means nets or snares. Charles read "scourges."
b: Ge'ez mäśagər is usually a net or a trap, the hunter's tool for catching animals. Charles translated "scourges." Nets fit the Bible's picture of God catching the wicked like animals (Ezekiel 12:13; 32:3; Hosea 7:12). The angels carry nets and chains to catch the fallen angels' "chosen and beloved ones" (56:3).

a: their own chosen and beloved ones
p: Probably the giants, the sons of the fallen angels.
b: "Their chosen and beloved ones" most likely means the children of the fallen angels, the giants (7:2; 10:9–12), whom their fathers will see destroyed (10:12; 12:6; 14:6). Others think it means the human followers of the angels, or the wicked kings of 56:5. Either way, the valley is the place where the angels' plan for a race of their own ends.

a: on the Parthians and the Medes
p: The one clear historical name in the Parables, and a clue to its date.
b: The Parthians ruled Iran and Mesopotamia from about 247 BC to AD 224. In 40 BC a Parthian army invaded Syria and Judea, took Jerusalem and put Antigonus, a Hasmonean prince, on the throne, until Herod retook the city with Roman help in 37 BC (Josephus, Jewish Antiquities 14.330–369). Many scholars think this passage remembers that invasion and dates the Parables after 40 BC. Others think it reflects Ezekiel 38–39's attack from the north, or Trajan's Parthian war of AD 113–117 (Hindley, who dated the Parables to about AD 115–117), and so it is not a precise clue.

a: the city of my righteous ones will trip up their horses
t: The city that cannot be taken
p: Jerusalem stands, and the attackers turn on one another.
b: The prophets picture enemies marching on Jerusalem and failing: "The sword of each man will be against his brother" (Ezekiel 38:21); "Each man will grab his neighbor's hand, and then raise his own hand against it" (Zechariah 14:13). "A son will not know his father" echoes the breakup of families before the end (Micah 7:6; Mark 13:12). If 56:5 remembers 40 BC, the writer is promising that the next invasion will fail.
r: Ezekiel 38:21; Zechariah 14:2–3; Zechariah 14:13; Micah 7:6; Mark 13:12; Revelation 20:9

a: Sheol will open its mouth
p: Like Korah's rebels, swallowed alive.
b: "The earth opened its mouth and swallowed them up" (Numbers 16:32), and "Sheol has made its throat wider and opened its mouth with no limit" (Isaiah 5:14). Here Sheol swallows the attackers "in front of the chosen ones," who see justice done. Sheol, the world of the dead, acts here as an agent of God's judgment on the invaders.

a: another army, of wagons
t: The wagons from east and west
p: Most read it as the scattered Jews coming home.
b: Right after the attack of 56:5–8 comes a second army, of wagons, from east and west, and all fall down and worship. Most scholars see the return of the scattered people of Israel, a hope of the prophets: "they will bring all your relatives from all the nations... on horses, in chariots and wagons" (Isaiah 66:20; compare Isaiah 27:13; Baruch 5:5–9). Others think it is a second wave of attackers, who are struck down.

a: Blessed are you, the righteous and the chosen
t: A blessing to open the third parable
p: A beatitude, the form Jesus uses in the Sermon on the Mount.
b: "Blessed are you..." is a beatitude, a form common in the Psalms (Psalm 1:1) and in Jewish wisdom. Jesus' Beatitudes promise the kingdom, comfort and the earth to the humble (Matthew 5:3–12). The third parable begins the same way, with the reward of the faithful before the judgment scenes.

a: in the light of eternal life
p: The righteous live in endless light.
b: Daniel 12:2 speaks of "everlasting life," and Daniel 12:3 of the wise shining like the sky. Isaiah 60:19–20 says the LORD will be an everlasting light. John's Gospel joins the two: "in him was life, and the life was humanity's light" (John 1:4). Revelation 22:5 says there will be no more night.

a: They showed me the dwellings of the dry land
p: Charles changed it to "judgments on the earth." The Ge'ez says "dwellings."
b: The Ge'ez has maḫdärat, "dwellings." Charles thought the word made no sense here and emended it to read "the judgments executed on the earth." The Plain keeps the Ethiopic texts. Thunder may be pictured as speaking over the places where people live, either to bless them or to curse them. Many scholars think chapter 59 is a later addition to the third parable.

a: in the life of Enoch
p: The date fits Noah, who was 500 in Genesis 5:32. The Ethiopic texts say Enoch.
b: Enoch lived 365 years (Genesis 5:23), so "the five hundredth year" does not fit him. It fits Noah: "When Noah was 500 years old" (Genesis 5:32). 60:8 also has the speaker call Enoch his grandfather. Charles suggested in his commentary that the passage first meant Noah, but he still printed "Enoch." The Ethiopic texts available to us (Dillmann and the EOTC Bible) read "Enoch," probably because an editor fitted a Noah vision into Enoch's book.

a: the heaven of heavens
p: The highest heaven, as in Deuteronomy 10:14.
b: The same Hebrew phrase stands behind "the sky belongs to the LORD your God, even the highest heavens" (Deuteronomy 10:14), and Solomon says that "the heavens above the heavens" are not big enough for God (1 Kings 8:27). It means the highest heaven, where God's throne is. 71:5 uses it again for Enoch's last ascent. Paul speaks of "the third heaven" (2 Corinthians 12:2).

a: My hips gave way and went limp, my insides melted
p: The prophets also collapse before God's glory.
b: Daniel lost all strength and fell on his face (Daniel 8:17–18; 10:8–9). Isaiah says "my hips are filled with pain" at a terrible vision (Isaiah 21:3). John writes, "I fell down at his feet like a dead man" (Revelation 1:17). In each case an angel or the Lord lifts the seer up, as here in 60:4.

a: for those who bow to the righteous judgment
p: Charles added "not." Without it the list includes the righteous too.
b: The Ge'ez says the day is prepared "for those who bow to (or worship) the righteous judgment, for those who deny the righteous judgment, and for those who take his name in vain." Charles added a "not" to the first phrase, making all three groups sinners. Without it the sentence is awkward, since the "power, punishment and judgment" seem to fall on the faithful, and most translators supply the "not." The Plain keeps the Ethiopic. It can be read only if the end of the verse applies to each group in turn: a covenant for the first group (the chosen) and an inquiry for the others.

a: take his name in vain
p: The third of the Ten Words.
b: "You must not take up the name of the LORD your God for something empty" (Exodus 20:7, in the Ten Commandments). The Ge'ez yanäśʾu səmo bäkä has the same picture: taking up the name "in vain," for an empty or false purpose such as a false oath. In 69:13–25 the oath and the hidden name are the power that holds the world together.

a: a female monster named Leviathan
p: The sea monster and the land monster, first named in Job.
b: God shows Job Behemoth (Job 40:15) and asks, "Will you haul Leviathan up on a fishhook?" (Job 41:1). Leviathan is also the sea serpent God crushes (Psalm 74:14; Isaiah 27:1). The Ugaritic myths of Syria, older than the Bible, tell of Baal defeating the sea serpent Lotan. Enoch makes Leviathan female and Behemoth male, and sends them to sea and desert. 4 Ezra 6:49–52 and 2 Baruch 29:4 say they were made on the fifth day and will be food for the righteous at the end.

a: Behemoth
p: Hebrew for "beast" in the plural of greatness: the Beast of beasts.
b: Ge'ez Bəḥemot comes from Hebrew behemot, the plural of behemah, "beast": a huge plural, "the great beast." In Job 40 he is a grass-eating giant, often read as the hippopotamus. Here he holds a desert called Dendayn (Ge'ez Dendayn; the meaning is unknown) east of Eden.

a: the place where my grandfather was taken up
p: Enoch was taken to a garden east of Eden. Genesis says only "God took him."
b: The speaker is Noah, Enoch's great-grandson (Genesis 5:21–29). Ge'ez ʾəmḥew means "grandfather" but is used loosely for any forefather. Genesis 5:24 does not say where God took Enoch. Enoch places him in the garden "where the chosen and the righteous live" (also 70:3–4; 106:8). Jubilees 4:23 puts him in the Garden of Eden, writing down the judgment. These are traditions that go beyond the 66 books.

a: You, son of man
t: "Son of man" as a plain address
p: Here it means "human being," the way God addresses Ezekiel.
b: The angel calls the seer wäldä säbʾ, the same words as "that Son of Man" in 46:2. But here it is only an address to a human being, as God calls Ezekiel "son of man" more than ninety times (Ezekiel 2:1) and Daniel is addressed in Daniel 8:17. The Plain uses a small "s" here. The angel's point: a mere human is trying to know what is hidden.

a: the storehouses of the winds
p: Chapter 60 lists the spirits that run the weather: an ancient science.
b: Verses 11–22 are a list of the weather and the angel or spirit in charge of each: winds, thunder, lightning, sea, frost, hail, snow, mist, dew and rain. Jubilees 2:2 says God created "the angels of the spirit of the winds... the spirits of the clouds, darkness, snow, hail and frost" on the first day. Revelation has four angels holding back the four winds (Revelation 7:1) and an angel in charge of the waters (Revelation 16:5).
r: Jubilees 2:2; Revelation 7:1; Revelation 14:18; Revelation 16:5; Psalm 104:4; Job 38:22–30

a: the spirit of the hail is a good angel
p: The Bible says God sends the weather. Enoch adds an angel for each kind.
b: The Psalms say God "makes the winds into his messengers" (Psalm 104:4) and that fire, hail, snow and storm "do his word" (Psalm 148:8). Enoch makes these spirits into angels, each with a task. Christians have read this either as a picture of God's providence, or as speculation that goes beyond Scripture. Hebrews 1:7 quotes Psalm 104:4 but stresses that the Son is greater than the angels.

a: will feed
t: Will they feed or be fed?
p: The monsters either feed (on sinners) or are food (for the righteous).
b: The Ge'ez yəsesäyu can be read "they will feed" or "they will be fed." Charles thought text was missing after it. Later Jewish writings say Leviathan and Behemoth will be food for the righteous at the end (4 Ezra 6:52; 2 Baruch 29:4; Talmud, Bava Batra 74b–75a). The next words, about children killed with their mothers, suggest instead that the monsters serve God's punishment. The verse is damaged and uncertain.

a: long cords
p: Angels measure the place of the righteous, as in Ezekiel and Zechariah.
b: A man with a measuring line measures the new temple in Ezekiel 40:3 and Jerusalem in Zechariah 2:1–5; John is told to measure the temple (Revelation 11:1), and an angel measures the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:15). Measuring marks something as God's, protected and set apart. Here the cords measure out the place of the chosen (70:3) and even find the dead who were lost (61:5).

a: those who were destroyed by the desert, and those who were eaten by the fish of the sea and by the wild animals
p: Even the dead with no grave will be found and raised.
b: Ancient people feared that those who died at sea or were eaten by animals could not be raised, since nothing was left to bury. The Parables answer: God's measures reach them too. Revelation 20:13 says "the sea gave up the dead who were in it." Early Christian writers such as Athenagoras (On the Resurrection) argued the same point against pagan objections.

a: they blessed that one
p: "That one" may be the Lord of Spirits or the Chosen One.
b: The Ge'ez says the heavenly beings bless "that one" (läwəʾətu) with their first words, without naming him. Most translators think it is the Lord of Spirits. Some think it is the Chosen One, who is enthroned in the next verse. If so, the angels praise him as they praise God, which Christian readers compare with Hebrews 1:6: "And let all the angels of God bow down to him."

a: The Lord of Spirits seated the Chosen One on the throne of his glory
p: God gives his own throne to the Chosen One, as in Psalm 110.
b: "The LORD declares to my lord: 'Sit at my right hand'" (Psalm 110:1), the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes most often about Jesus (Mark 14:62; Acts 2:34–35; Hebrews 1:13). Revelation has the Lamb share God's throne (Revelation 3:21; 22:1). Here the Chosen One sits on God's throne and judges even the holy ones of heaven.

a: the cherubim, the seraphim and the ophanim
p: Three kinds of angels around the throne.
b: The cherubim guard Eden and carry God's throne (Genesis 3:24; Ezekiel 10). The seraphim, "burning ones," sing in Isaiah 6:2–3. The ophanim, "wheels" (Hebrew ofannim), are the wheels full of eyes in Ezekiel 1:15–21, which later Jewish writers treated as a class of angel. 71:7 names the same three. Jewish and Christian lists of angel ranks grew from passages like this.

a: the angels of the dominions
p: Enoch lists orders of angels, as Paul names "thrones, lordships, rulers, authorities."
b: Ge'ez ʾagaʾəzt means "lordships, dominions." Paul says that in Christ were created "thrones or lordships or rulers or authorities" (Colossians 1:16; compare Ephesians 1:21). Later Christian writers, above all Pseudo-Dionysius in the 500s, arranged the angels into nine choirs. The Bible gives the names but not the ranking, which goes beyond it.

a: the garden of life
p: Paradise as the home of the righteous.
b: The "garden of life" is Eden renewed, where the tree of life grows (Genesis 2:9; Revelation 2:7; 22:2). In 60:8 and 60:23 it is "the garden of the righteous." Jesus promises the thief, "Today you will be with me in paradise" (Luke 23:43); "paradise" is a Persian word for a walled garden.

a: lift up your horns
p: A horn stands for strength and pride.
b: In the Psalms "horn" means strength: "Do not lift your horn on high" is a warning to the proud (Psalm 75:4–5). God tells the kings to raise their horns, a challenge: show your power, if you can recognize the Chosen One. They cannot.

a: The word of his mouth kills all the sinners
p: Isaiah 11:4, also used of Christ in 2 Thessalonians and Revelation.
b: "His mouth will be a rod to strike the earth, and the breath of his lips will put the wicked to death" (Isaiah 11:4). Paul says the Lord Jesus will do away with the lawless one "by the breath of his mouth" (2 Thessalonians 2:8), and in Revelation a sword comes out of the rider's mouth (Revelation 19:15). If the verse speaks of the Chosen One, as most translators think (see the note on "on him"), then with 49:3 (Isaiah 11:2) the Parables make him the king of Isaiah 11.

a: The spirit of righteousness was poured out on him
p: With "sat," "him" and "his mouth" are God; with "seated him," the Chosen One.
b: The printed Ethiopic texts say the Lord of Spirits sat on the throne, so read strictly, "on him" and "his mouth" in this verse mean God. Most translators (Charles; Nickelsburg and VanderKam, who mark it) change "sat" to "seated him", and then the spirit and the word of the mouth belong to the Chosen One, as in 49:3 and 61:8. 62:3 and 62:5, where the kings see the Son of Man on the throne, fit the second reading better. See the variant.

a: like the pain of a woman in labor
p: The prophets' picture of sudden, unescapable fear.
b: "Cramps and pains will grip them; they will writhe like a woman giving birth" (Isaiah 13:8). Paul says destruction will come on the careless "like birth pains on a woman who is pregnant. And there will be no escape for them" (1 Thessalonians 5:3). Jesus calls the troubles before the end "the start of the labor pains" (Mark 13:8).

a: when they see that Son of a Woman
t: The Son of Man on his throne and the Gospels
p: The Parables and Matthew share a rare picture. Who borrowed from whom?
b: The kings see the Son of Man "sitting on the throne of his glory." Jesus speaks of the time "when the world is born again and the Son of Man takes his seat on the throne of his glory" (Matthew 19:28), and says, "When the Son of Man comes in his glory... then he will take his seat on the throne of his glory" (Matthew 25:31). Views: (1) the Parables are Jewish and earlier, and Matthew or Jesus knew their language (many, though not all, who date the Parables early); (2) both draw on Daniel 7 and Jewish speech without depending on each other (Casey); (3) the Son of Man passages are Christian additions to Enoch, or the whole book is Christian (Milik, and older scholars). Against (3), a Christian writer would hardly make Enoch the Son of Man (71:14). The Ethiopian Orthodox church reads the vision as Enoch's prophecy of Christ.

a: the Son of Man was hidden
p: The second Ge'ez phrase, the one most used from here on.
b: Here the Ge'ez is wäldä ʾəgʷalä ʾəmmäḥəyaw, literally "son of the offspring of the mother of the living." "The mother of the living" is Eve (Genesis 3:20), so the phrase means "son of humankind." It stands in 62:7, 9, 14; 63:11; 69:26–27; 70:1; 71:17. The Ethiopic New Testament uses the same phrase for Jesus' title "the Son of Man." On the first phrase see 46:2; on the third, 69:29.

a: put their hope in that Son of Man
p: The kings' plea comes too late. Elsewhere Scripture invites the nations to hope in God's king.
b: Psalm 2:10–12 calls the kings of the earth to be wise and "kiss the son" before his anger flares; Isaiah 42:4 says "the islands are waiting for his teaching." Here the kings do worship and hope, but too late: the Lord of Spirits drives them away (62:10). Christian readers compare Matthew 25:41–46 and Luke 13:25, where those shut out knock in vain.

a: the sword of the Lord of Spirits is drunk on them
p: A fierce prophetic image of judgment.
b: "My sword has drunk deep in the heavens" (Isaiah 34:5); "I will make my arrows drunk with blood, / and my sword will eat flesh" (Deuteronomy 32:42). The Ge'ez says only that the sword is drunk "from them"; the word "blood" in many versions is supplied. The righteous rejoice at the sight. Modern readers often find this troubling. The Bible too speaks of joy at God's justice (Psalm 58:10; Revelation 18:20; 19:1–3), while Jesus also teaches love for enemies (Matthew 5:44).
r: Isaiah 34:5–6; Deuteronomy 32:42; Jeremiah 46:10; Psalm 58:10; Revelation 19:1–3; Matthew 5:44

a: and eat, and lie down and get up, forever and ever
t: Eating with the Son of Man
p: The great feast of the age to come.
b: Isaiah 25:6 promises a feast for all peoples on God's mountain. Jesus says many "will come from the sunrise and the sunset and lie down to eat with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven" (Matthew 8:11), and Revelation 19:9 blesses those invited to the wedding supper of the Lamb. The EOTC text reads "eat and drink." Many Christian readers connect such promises with the Lord's Supper, which looks ahead to that feast (1 Corinthians 11:26).

a: they will have put on the clothing of life
p: The resurrection body pictured as new clothes.
b: Paul says we groan, "longing to be dressed over with our dwelling from heaven," so that "life may swallow up what is mortal" (2 Corinthians 5:2–4), and the perishable must "put on" the imperishable (1 Corinthians 15:53). Revelation gives the faithful white robes (Revelation 3:5; 7:9). In Isaiah 61:10 God clothes his people in "garments of salvation." Charles's text reads "garments of glory" here; Dillmann's has "life."

a: the Lord of kings
p: The kings finally admit who is above them.
b: Nebuchadnezzar calls Daniel's God "the God of gods and the lord of kings" (Daniel 2:47). Revelation calls the Lamb "Lord of lords and King of kings" (Revelation 17:14; 19:16), and 1 Timothy 6:15 uses it of God. The kings' hymn here (63:2–4) is correct, but it comes too late to help them.

a: His judgments show no favoritism
p: Literally, "his judgments do not lift the face."
b: To "lift the face" of someone is a Hebrew idiom for showing favor or taking a bribe (Leviticus 19:15; Deuteronomy 10:17). God "shows no partiality" (Deuteronomy 10:17; Acts 10:34; Romans 2:11). The kings, used to being favored, find that this judge cannot be bought.

a: the wealth of wrongdoing
p: The phrase behind Jesus' "unrighteous mammon" (Luke 16:9).
b: The Ge'ez nəway ʿämäḍa, "possessions of wrongdoing," matches the phrase Jesus uses in Luke 16:9, "the mammon of unrighteousness" (KJV), meaning money gained or used unjustly. Both probably go back to a Hebrew or Aramaic phrase with mamon, "wealth." The Dead Sea Scrolls speak of "wealth of wickedness" too (Damascus Document 6:15). The kings find that their money does not keep them out of Sheol.

a: the sword will stay before his face among them
p: The judgment scene of the second section ends with the kings shut out.
b: Chapters 62–63 are the longest judgment scene in 1 Enoch. Most scholars see in it a picture of the writers' own oppressors. The scene of rulers begging, then shut out into darkness, is close to Wisdom of Solomon 5:1–13, where the wicked see the righteous they despised now exalted and confess, "So we strayed from the way of truth."

a: These are the angels who came down from heaven to the earth
p: A short reminder of the Watchers' story in chapters 6–16.
b: This one-verse vision sums up the sin of the Watchers: they came down, revealed hidden things, and led people into sin (see 6:1–8; 8:1–4; 16:3). Revealing secrets is the main charge in the Parables (65:6–11; 69:1–12). Genesis 6:1–4 says only that the sons of God took wives; the teaching of forbidden arts is Enoch's addition.

a: In those days Noah saw
p: Chapters 65–69 are told by Noah, not Enoch.
b: 65:1–3 tells of Noah in the third person. From 65:4 Noah speaks in the first person, through 68:1, and Enoch is his "grandfather" (strictly, great-grandfather; see 60:8). The scene is like 106–107, where Methuselah goes to Enoch "at the ends of the earth" to ask about baby Noah. Most scholars think these sections come from a lost Book of Noah (see 54:7). The Ethiopian church reads them as part of Enoch's book, which itself says that Enoch passed his writings to Noah (68:1).

a: the earth had tilted
p: A cosmic sign before the Flood.
b: The Ge'ez ʾadnänät means "leaned, bent down." A tilting earth is a sign of the world's order coming apart, like the earth that "staggers like a drunkard" in Isaiah 24:20. In 80:2–7 the sky goes out of order in the days of sinners.

a: the power of those who cast metal idols for the whole earth
p: The Parables blame fallen angels for magic and idols. The Bible bans them without saying who taught them.
b: The list (secrets of angels, sorcery, spells, idols, metalwork) matches what Azazel and the Watchers teach in 8:1–3. The law of Moses forbids sorcery and idols (Exodus 22:18; Deuteronomy 18:10–12; Exodus 20:4), and Isaiah mocks the smith who casts an idol (Isaiah 40:19; 44:9–20). Enoch goes further than the Bible by tracing these arts to angels. Genesis 4:22 credits metalwork to Tubal-cain, a human, without blame.

a: Because of the months they searched out and learned
p: The Ge'ez says "months." Charles read "sorceries."
b: Dillmann's text has ʾäwraḫ, "months" or "moons." Charles thought it made no sense and read "sorceries," assuming a mix-up in the Greek. But the Enochic books care a great deal about the calendar: in 8:3 the Watchers teach "the signs of the moon," and in 80:2–8 sinners go wrong by following the moon. The crime may be learning the courses of the moon for fortune-telling.

a: From your offspring will flow a spring of the righteous
p: Noah's line will carry the righteous through the Flood.
b: "Noah found favor in the LORD's eyes" (Genesis 6:8), and God promised to keep his offspring (Genesis 9:9). In 10:3 and 10:16 God promises a "plant of righteousness" from Noah. The promise of "kings" may look ahead to Abraham's line (Genesis 17:6) and David.

a: not to raise their hands, but to keep watch
t: Angels who hold back the Flood
p: The waters are held back until Noah is ready.
b: The angels over the waters are told to wait. Revelation 7:1–3 has four angels holding back the winds until God's servants are sealed. 1 Peter 3:20 speaks of the time "when God's patience was waiting in the days of Noah, while the ark was being made ready." Enoch makes that patience a command to angels.

a: the angels are making something of wood
p: In Genesis, Noah builds the ark. Here angels build it.
b: Genesis 6:14 says, "Make yourself an ark of gopher wood," and Noah does it (Genesis 6:22; Hebrews 11:7). The Ge'ez here says the angels are making the wooden thing, perhaps to stress that the rescue is God's work. This goes beyond, and differs in detail from, Genesis.

a: They will lock up those angels who showed wrongdoing in that burning valley
p: Noah refers back to the burning valley of 54:1–6.
b: The verb is plural, "they will shut them up," meaning the angels of punishment (Charles has "He"). Noah says his grandfather had shown him this valley before, in the west among the mountains of metal (52:2; 54:1). The fallen angels are kept there until the last judgment. 2 Peter 2:4 says "God did not spare the angels who sinned. He threw them into Tartarus and handed them over to chains of gloom," and Jude 6 is close.

a: for healing soul and body, but for punishing the spirit
p: Healing springs that become fire: perhaps the springs where Herod sought a cure.
b: Volcanic hot springs with a sulfur smell rise near the Dead Sea, at Callirrhoe on its east shore. Josephus tells how Herod the Great, dying in 4 BC, went there to bathe, without success (Jewish War 1.657; Jewish Antiquities 17.171). Many scholars see the "kings" who use these healing waters as Herod and his family, and so date the Parables to Herod's time or soon after. Others say any ruler could visit the springs, so the clue is weaker than it looks.

a: deny the Spirit of the Lord
p: Close to the Gospels' warning about the sin against the Holy Spirit.
b: The kings "deny the Spirit of the Lord" while they see their punishment daily (67:8). Jesus warns that blasphemy against the Holy Spirit will not be forgiven (Mark 3:28–29; Matthew 12:31–32). Enoch does not use the phrase in the same way, but both describe a hardened refusal to see God's hand. Elsewhere the Parables say "the Lord of Spirits"; here "the Spirit of the Lord" is singular.

a: a fire that burns forever
p: The waters of healing will become everlasting fire.
b: "Their worm will not die, and their fire will not be put out" (Isaiah 66:24, quoted in Mark 9:48). Jude 7 speaks of Sodom undergoing "the punishment of eternal fire," and Revelation of "the lake of fire and sulfur" (Revelation 20:10). The Parables join sulfur (67:6), fire and water in one picture.

a: for the healing of the angels
p: A crux: the Ge'ez says the waters heal "the angels"; Charles made it "the kings."
b: Dillmann's text reads läfäwsä ziʾähomu lämälaʾəkt wälämotä śəgahomu, "for the healing of the angels and for the death of their body"; the EOTC Bible has "the body of the angels." Neither has "kings" or "lust." Charles thought healing for angels made no sense in a passage about the kings (67:8–12) and emended the line. The Plain keeps the Ethiopic. It may mean the waters are judgment for both the angels and their human allies, or the text may be damaged. See the variant.

a: He put them together for me in the words of the book of the parables
t: How Enoch's books were handed down
p: Enoch gives his books to Noah. The book tells its own story of transmission.
b: 1 Enoch explains how writings from before the Flood reached later readers: Enoch hands them to Methuselah (82:1–3; 92:1), and here to Noah. Jubilees 10:14 and 21:10 also have books passed down through Noah. This is how the book answers the obvious question of how anything Enoch wrote could survive the Flood. Ethiopian Orthodox teachers accept this account; most scholars see it as a device of the later writers.

a: they act as if they were the Lord
p: The angels' sin is pride: acting as if they were God.
b: Michael refuses to plead for the fallen angels because they "act as if they were the Lord" (literally "in the likeness of the Lord"). The proud king of Isaiah 14:14 says, "I will make myself the Most High's equal," and Christian tradition has often read that verse and Ezekiel 28 as the fall of Satan. Scripture itself does not clearly say so; Enoch's phrase fits that later reading.

a: the first of them is Shemihazah
p: A second list of the Watchers' chiefs, close to the one in 6:7.
b: The Ge'ez Səmyaza is Shemihazah, the Watchers' leader in 6:3. The list roughly matches 6:7, though many names are spelled differently, and Azazel, tenth here, is tenth in 6:7 too, as ʾAsaʾel (Aramaic ʿAsaʾel), the figure whom the Ethiopic of 8:1 and the Parables call Azazel. Several names end in -el, "God": Kokabel "star of God," Baraqel "lightning of God," Ananel "cloud of God" (compare 8:3). The Aramaic of 6:7 survives at Qumran (4Q201), which helps scholars correct the Ethiopic spellings; for chapter 69 there is no such help.

a: led them astray through the daughters of humans
p: Genesis 6:2.
b: "The sons of God saw that the daughters of humankind were good to look at, and they took wives for themselves from all of them, whomever they chose" (Genesis 6:2). Here a single angel, Yeqon, leads the rest astray, and Asbeel advises them (69:5). Yeqon may mean "he will rise up"; Asbeel may mean "God has forsaken."

a: He led Eve astray
p: Enoch names a fallen angel, Gadreel, as Eve's tempter. Genesis speaks of a snake.
b: Genesis 3 says "the snake" deceived the woman: "The snake fooled me, and I ate" (Genesis 3:13). It does not say an angel was behind it. Later Jewish and Christian writers linked the snake with the devil (Wisdom of Solomon 2:24; Revelation 12:9; 2 Corinthians 11:3). Enoch is unusual in naming another angel, Gadreel ("God is my wall"?), who also teaches war. This goes beyond Genesis; most churches teach the snake was Satan's instrument but do not follow Enoch's naming.
r: Genesis 3:1–13; Wisdom of Solomon 2:24; 2 Corinthians 11:3; Revelation 12:9; 1 Timothy 2:14

a: He taught people to write with ink and papyrus
p: A strange claim inside a book that is all about writing.
b: Penemue teaches writing, and 69:10 says people were not made to confirm their faith "with pen and ink." This is odd in a book where Enoch is "the scribe of righteousness" (12:4) and angels write in heavenly books. Scholars suggest the target is written oaths and contracts, which replaced a person's word, or secret magical writing. The 66 books treat writing as good: God writes the Ten Words (Exodus 31:18) and tells Moses and the prophets to write (Exodus 17:14; Habakkuk 2:2).

a: people were created no differently from the angels
p: Without this knowledge, death would not have touched humans.
b: The verse says humans were meant to stay pure and deathless like the angels, and death came through forbidden knowledge. Wisdom of Solomon 2:23–24 says, "God created us for incorruption... but through the devil's envy death entered the world." Genesis 2:17 and Romans 5:12 tie death to sin. Enoch blames knowledge taught by angels; Genesis and Paul blame human disobedience. The words "it is devouring me" are puzzling; some think the scribe slipped, others that Noah speaks of his own mortality.
r: Genesis 2:17; Wisdom of Solomon 2:23–24; Romans 5:12; Psalm 8:5; Luke 20:36

a: the blows that strike in the heat of noon
p: Psalm 91's "destruction that wastes at noon."
b: Psalm 91:6 promises protection from "the plague that creeps through the dark" and "the destruction that ruins at noon." The Greek Old Testament turns the second into "the demon of noon," and later monks spoke of the "noonday demon" of boredom. Kasdeya teaches the blows of demons: miscarriage, snakebite and sunstroke. "Tabaet" is the Ge'ez word for "male," so the name may mean "the strong one."

a: the number of Kasbeel
p: The Ge'ez word means "number." Its sense here is uncertain.
b: Ge'ez ḫʷəlqʷ normally means "number, count." Charles read "the task of Kasbeel." Some think it is a code for the secret name, whose letters add up to a number, as names did in Jewish and Greek number games (compare Revelation 13:18). Kasbeel is "the chief of the oath," and the oath, named Beqa and Akae, is the subject of 69:13–25. These words have no clear meaning in Ge'ez and may be garbled Hebrew or Aramaic.

a: Heaven was hung in place before the world was created
t: The world held by an oath
p: The poem of the oath echoes Job 38 and Proverbs 8.
b: God set the sand as a boundary for the sea (Jeremiah 5:22), and asks Job who "put up a bolt and doors" for it and said, "Up to here you may come, but not one step more" (Job 38:10–11). Proverbs 8:27–29 has Wisdom present when God fixed the heavens and gave the sea its limit. Here the power that holds it all is a sworn oath and a secret name. Later Jewish mystical texts speak of the divine name sealing creation.

a: because the name of that Son of Man had been revealed to them
p: The ending is abrupt. Scholars think something has fallen out.
b: "They" have no clear subject: perhaps the righteous, perhaps the angels or the forces of nature just named. The return to the Son of Man is sudden after the Noah material. Most scholars think 69:26–29 is the real end of the third parable, which the Noah sections interrupted. Ethiopian readers take it as the joyful close of the vision of judgment.

a: the whole of judgment was given to him
t: All judgment given to the Son
p: John 5:22, 27: the Father gives judgment to the Son because he is "son of man."
b: Ge'ez rəʾsä kʷənnane, "the head, the sum of judgment," means all of it. Jesus says, "The Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son," and has given him authority to judge "because he is the Son of Man" (John 5:22, 27). In Daniel 7:14 the son of man receives authority and kingdom; the Parables make that authority judgment.

a: that Son of Man has appeared
p: The third Ge'ez phrase, used here and in 71:14.
b: Here the Ge'ez is wäldä bəʾəsi, "son of a man" (bəʾəsi means a man, a male person). It appears twice in this verse and again in 71:14, where Enoch is called this. Some think the change of phrase means nothing; others that it marks a different source or translator. On the other two phrases see 46:2 and 62:7; on "son of a woman" see 62:5. Charles thought the three phrases were simply different ways to render the one Greek phrase behind them.

a: This is the third parable of Enoch
t: The end of the third parable
p: The book of three parables closes. Chapters 70–71 are an epilogue.
b: The third parable began at 58:1. Chapters 70–71 tell how Enoch himself was taken up, and many scholars treat them as an epilogue, perhaps added by a later hand. That question matters for 71:14, since a later ending could change who the Son of Man is.

a: while he was still alive
p: The Parables' version of Genesis 5:24.
b: Genesis says Enoch "was gone, for God took him" (Genesis 5:24). Hebrews 11:5 says, "By faith Enoch was carried off, so that he did not see death." Here Enoch's "name" (meaning Enoch himself) is lifted up "alive." The text switches from "he" (70:1–2) to "I" (70:3), as if a narrator hands over to Enoch. Sirach 44:16 and 49:14 also praise Enoch as taken up.

a: on the chariots of the spirit
p: Like Elijah's chariot of fire.
b: "A chariot of fire and horses of fire" parted Elijah and Elisha, "and Elijah went up to the heavens in the windstorm" (2 Kings 2:11). Jewish tradition paired Enoch and Elijah as the two who did not die, and some church fathers took them to be the two witnesses of Revelation 11:3–12 (Tertullian, On the Soul 50).

a: the first fathers
p: The righteous ancestors, already in the garden.
b: "The first fathers" are probably the righteous before the Flood, such as Adam, Seth and Enosh, who live with the righteous in the garden. Jesus speaks of Abraham, Isaac and Jacob alive before God (Mark 12:26–27), and Hebrews 12:23 of "the spirits of the righteous made perfect."

a: walking on flames of fire
p: Ministers who are "flames of fire."
b: God "makes his messengers winds, his servants flames of fire" (Psalm 104:4; Hebrews 1:7). Daniel's throne is "flames of fire" with a river of fire flowing from it (Daniel 7:9–10). White clothes and faces like snow mark heavenly beings (Daniel 10:6; Matthew 28:3).

a: like jacinth
p: A blue or red-orange gemstone.
b: Ge'ez yakənt is the Greek hyakinthos, a precious stone, blue or reddish. It is the eleventh foundation stone of the new Jerusalem (Revelation 21:20), and the color of the riders' breastplates in Revelation 9:17. The fire of heaven shines like a jewel, as in the throne visions of Ezekiel 1.

a: a house built of crystal stones
p: The heavenly temple, as in the Book of the Watchers.
b: This repeats Enoch's first ascent, where he sees a house of hailstones and fire, and a greater house beyond it with God's throne (14:9–23). Ge'ez ʾäsḥätya means frost or ice, here crystal. Ezekiel 1:22 has a platform "like awesome ice" above the living creatures; Revelation 4:6 a sea of glass like crystal before the throne.

a: Then the spirit carried Enoch off
p: The story shifts from "I" to "Enoch" and back.
b: The narrator says "Enoch" here and "I" in the next phrase. The same shifts occur in 39:2 and 70:1–3. Some scholars see the hand of an editor joining pieces. Others think it is a deliberate style for a holy man speaking of his own ascent; Paul does something similar in 2 Corinthians 12:2–4 ("I know a man in Christ").

a: His head was white and pure like wool
p: Daniel 7:9, the vision of chapter 46 repeated.
b: "His clothing was white, like snow, and the hair of his head was like clean wool" (Daniel 7:9). The scene returns to 46:1, where Enoch first saw the Head of Days with the Son of Man. But here no second figure is described beside God, and Charles believed a passage had dropped out.

a: my spirit was changed
p: Enoch is changed before he is told who he is.
b: Enoch's body "went limp," Ge'ez "melted," and his spirit was "changed." Some read this as Enoch being changed into a heavenly being, ready for 71:14; later Jewish tradition made Enoch into the great angel Metatron (3 Enoch 3–16). Others read it as the usual collapse of a seer (60:3; Daniel 10:8). Paul says "all of us will be changed" (1 Corinthians 15:51).

a: You are the Son of Man who was born for righteousness
t: Is Enoch the Son of Man?
p: The most debated verse in 1 Enoch. Here an angel tells Enoch that he is the Son of Man.
b: The Ethiopic texts available to us (Dillmann and the EOTC Bible) say, "You are the Son of Man." Views: (1) Enoch is the Son of Man of chapters 46–69, revealed at last and installed in heaven (VanderKam, Olson). (2) Chapter 71 is a later addition that identifies Enoch with a figure who in 46–69 was someone else (Collins; Nickelsburg). (3) The phrase here means only "a human being": "you are a man born for righteousness," not the title (Casey). (4) Charles changed the text to "This is the Son of Man," with no manuscript support. Christian readers who see Christ in the Son of Man of 46–69 must decide how this verse fits; we know of no official Ethiopian Orthodox statement on it. One of the main arguments that the Parables are Jewish is that a Christian writer would hardly have written it.

a: in the name of the world to come
p: A Jewish phrase for the age after the judgment.
b: Ge'ez ʿaläm zäyəkäwwən, "the world that will be," is the Hebrew ha-olam ha-ba, "the world to come," a common rabbinic phrase. Jesus contrasts "this age" with "the age to come" (Matthew 12:32; Mark 10:30), and Hebrews 6:5 speaks of "the powers of the age to come."

a: So there will be long life with that Son of Man
p: The book closes with peace for the righteous.
b: The Parables end as they began, with the righteous and their reward (38:1–6). "Length of days" is the blessing of Psalm 21:4 and 91:16. The next book in 1 Enoch, the Astronomical Book (72–82), starts a new subject entirely: the courses of the sun, moon and stars. The jump shows that 1 Enoch is a collection of once separate books.
